clue.text: Bore with a little alcohol: a mouse could do it

definitions.note: a clause describing an action, standing for the phrase naming it

blocks.note: a bore, something tedious, is a drag
with means together with, and
a drop is a small drink

explanation.surface: A dull evening nursing a small drink, followed by the odd thought that a mouse could manage it.
explanation.walkthrough: The mouse is the computer kind, not a rodent; 'with' is doing real work as AND rather than joining.
explanation.definitionFit: With a computer mouse you click an item, pull it across the screen and let go, which is the standard interface action.

clue.text: Downed by an aggressive vehicle? That provides a sobering experience

blocks.note: a drink that has been downed has been drunk
a tank is an armoured fighting vehicle

explanation.surface: Someone flattened by a menacing vehicle would find the experience sobering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downed' reads as knocked over; here it is the past participle of drinking something down.
explanation.definitionFit: A police cell where intoxicated people are held overnight until they sober up, chiefly an American term.

clue.text: Advice to writers about clichés

definitions.note: the advice itself is the famous self-mocking rule, so the phrase fills the gap in it

blocks.note: surface reading: a style tip telling writers to steer clear of stock phrases
setter's reading: the well-known joke rule that itself uses a cliché while forbidding them

explanation.walkthrough: The joke writing rule is 'Avoid clichés like ...', which breaks itself by ending in a hackneyed simile; the answer is that phrase with the clichés word removed.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to shun something completely, and it is the classic self-contradicting tip in lists of writing rules.

clue.text: Cavities want rapid filling

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something, so the letters wanted lie within the words

blocks.note: spans the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A dentist's remark that holes in teeth need quick filling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filling' sounds dental, which suits the cavities, but it signals letters inside the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Antra is the plural of antrum, an anatomical term for a hollow chamber such as a sinus in bone.

clue.text: Retainer’s reduced earnings with staff finally cut

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: prices reduced are down
earnings are pay
staff are the men employed
the last letter of this word

explanation.surface: A servant finds wages trimmed and the rest of the household laid off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retainer' suggests an old family servant, but here it is money paid up front.
explanation.definitionFit: A retainer is a fee paid in advance to secure services, just as a deposit is paid up front toward a purchase.

clue.text: English flag has this contradictory signal for pedestrians?

blocks.note: first meaning: the St George flag of England is this emblem on white
second meaning: a red light says stop while the other word says go over

explanation.walkthrough: At a crossing a red figure means don't go; pairing that colour with the instruction to go over makes a mixed message.
explanation.definitionFit: England's flag is the cross of St George, a scarlet upright cross on a white field; the two words also form an impossible traffic instruction.

clue.text: Push free material for reporters

blocks.note: to push down is to press
to free is to release

explanation.surface: Pushing free handouts on journalists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' reads as costless material, but it is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: An official statement issued by an organisation to newspapers and broadcasters for them to publish.

clue.text: Classical puzzle that was solved at a stroke

definitions.text: Classical puzzle that was solved at a stroke

blocks.clueFragment: Classical puzzle that was solved at a stroke
blocks.note: surface reading: an ancient riddle that someone cracked in one flash of insight
setter's reading: literally cut through with one blow of a sword

explanation.walkthrough: 'At a stroke' means instantly, but in the legend Alexander the Great simply sliced the tangle with his sword.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary intricate knot at Gordium in Phrygia, which Alexander severed rather than untied, now any intractable problem.

clue.text: Snaps members of the Red Headed League?

definitions.text: members of the Red Headed League

blocks.note: first meaning: crisp spiced biscuits, also called ginger snaps

blocks.clueFragment: members of the Red Headed League
blocks.note: second meaning: redheads who are fanatics, a playful description

explanation.walkthrough: The Red-Headed League is a Sherlock Holmes story; its members would be redheads, and enthusiasts are nuts. Ginger nuts are a British biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: The biscuits are hard spiced cookies; in the second sense redheaded people are called gingers and devotees are called nuts.

clue.text: Carnivore from Africa, price one pound

blocks.note: a rate is a price charged
L is the symbol for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A market listing an African animal at a price of a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One pound' is a single unit, so it is just the one-letter abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The ratel is the honey badger, a fierce meat-eating mammal found across Africa and southern Asia.

clue.text: Traps one scholar, closing part of the Parthenon

indicators.note: closing on something shuts it inside, as a hand closes on a coin

blocks.note: Roman numeral one
a Master of Arts is a scholar
the triangular gable over the temple's columns

explanation.surface: A trap for an academic studying the Parthenon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Traps' looks like a verb, but it is a noun meaning belongings, as in 'pack up your traps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Traps is an informal word for personal belongings or luggage; impedimenta are baggage and equipment that slow travel.

clue.text: Naval officer nine places away from the PM?

definitions.text: nine places away from the PM
definitions.note: a cryptic description rather than a synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: the first lieutenant of a ship, informally

blocks.clueFragment: nine places away from the PM
blocks.note: second meaning: the Prime Minister lives at Number Ten, and nine down from ten is one

explanation.walkthrough: The PM is the British Prime Minister, whose residence is 10 Downing Street, so nine house numbers away gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Royal Navy the second-in-command of a vessel is nicknamed this; the second sense is a street address counted from Downing Street.

clue.text: Eggs with awful smell almost picked up

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
in a down entry, lifting letters upward makes them read bottom to top

blocks.note: a stink is a foul smell

explanation.surface: Eggs going off with a foul smell that someone nearly picks up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' tempts as a homophone signal; in a down clue it means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Nits are the eggs of lice, found clinging to hair, so the definition names them by their biology.

clue.text: Had weight disclosed

blocks.note: first meaning: had an effect
second meaning: revealed, related

explanation.walkthrough: 'Had weight' suggests scales; it is the sense of counting or having influence.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb tell can mean to have a marked effect or carry weight, and more commonly to reveal or relate information.

clue.text: Crafty killer in bar taking pressure off grass

definitions.note: a killer that is a craft, i.e. a vessel

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, and pressure is the letter abbreviation to go

blocks.note: a pub is a bar
the oat is a cereal grass

explanation.surface: A cunning murderer in a pub, easing off on an informer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' begs to be read as an informer; it is the plant family. P is the physics symbol for pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: A German submarine is a warship, a craft whose purpose is to sink others, hence a killer vessel.

clue.text: Wicket! I had gone, sadly for a duck

indicators.note: sadly suggests things went wrong, so the letters end up in disorder

blocks.note: W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wicket
the contraction I'd
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricketer out for nought: the wicket falls, and a duck is a score of zero.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of nothing, which the surface invokes; here it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The widgeon, also spelt wigeon, is a dabbling freshwater duck with a whistling call.

clue.text: Material for printer is empty, rubbished along with the rest

indicators.note: rubbished means trashed, so these letters are thrown into a mess

blocks.note: taken as written
et al, Latin for 'and the others'

explanation.surface: A printer's cartridge is empty and gets thrown out with everything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' looks like a description of the printer, but it supplies its own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The alloy of lead, tin and antimony used for casting movable type in traditional letterpress printing.

clue.text: Criminal also about to tuck into some breakfast?

indicators.note: about as in turning about, facing the other way
tucking into food puts it inside you, so one part goes within another

blocks.note: also means and
a kipper, a smoked herring, is a traditional British breakfast

explanation.surface: A crook who is also about to tuck into his breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tuck into' sounds like eating, which suits breakfast, but it means go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who abducts someone and holds them for ransom commits a serious crime.

clue.text: Walk, run, climb here

blocks.note: to step is to walk
a ladder is a run in a stocking

explanation.surface: An exercise instruction: walk, run, then climb.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make an athletic sequence, but 'run' is the snag in tights, called a ladder in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A folding set of steps is the thing you go up, so the place where you climb is the item itself.

clue.text: Enjoy love in a flowerbed? Grotesque!

blocks.note: to enjoy is to like
love is zero in tennis, so nothing
a plant in a bed sits in the soil

explanation.surface: Romance among the flowers, dismissed as grotesque.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' is not affection here but the tennis score of zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bizarre or hideous seems unlike anything in the world, which is what the idiom says.

clue.text: With soup, regularly refresh members of union

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: broth is a thin soup
the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Handing out soup to revive trade unionists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' here takes the even-numbered letters, not the odd ones; only that choice gives real letters that fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Trade unionists traditionally address fellow members as brother, a term of solidarity within the movement.

clue.text: Financial support some needed to secure expensive car

indicators.note: securing something holds it fast, so one part is gripped by another

blocks.note: any means some
a limo is a luxury limousine

explanation.surface: Money is needed as collateral to buy a luxury car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' is not a selection signal here; it is simply a synonym supplying the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Payments a court orders one former spouse to make to the other after divorce or separation.

clue.text: Officer in command, lazy on vacation

indicators.note: vacated means emptied, so the insides go and only the outside pair remains

blocks.note: an order is a command
first and last letters only

explanation.surface: The commanding officer is idle while away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' reads as being on holiday; it means emptied out.
explanation.definitionFit: The orderly officer is the military officer of the day, responsible for routine duties in a unit.

clue.text: Not so lenient as Lawrence King

blocks.note: Laurence Sterne, author of Tristram Shandy
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Comparing the strictness of a man named Lawrence and a king.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist usually spells his name Laurence; the clue uses the variant spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Stern means severe or strict, so its comparative describes someone harsher and less forgiving.

clue.text: Flushed with anger, court is to change jury instructions

blocks.note: a flushed face is red
ire is anger
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A judge goes red with fury and says the court must alter what it told the jury.

explanation.definitionFit: A judge directs a jury on the law, so issuing fresh directions means doing it again differently.

clue.text: More temperamental, and lower when girl interrupts

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so one part lands in the middle of another

Di, short for Diana

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' reads as more downcast, but it is a cow that lows, rhyming with slower.
explanation.definitionFit: Moody means given to sudden changes of mood, and the comparative describes someone even more changeable in temper.

clue.text: With calves under water, require to put board round

indicators.note: to put something round another is to surround it

blocks.note: to require is to need
board and keep both mean food and lodging

explanation.surface: Young cattle standing in a flood, and a plank is needed around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calves' suggests young cattle; it is the backs of the lower legs. Board is room and meals, as is keep.

clue.text: Person with an entitlement: vets resented it badly

blocks.note: the fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests animal doctors grumbling; 'vets' is just letters.

clue.text: Tram isn’t moving, so pass on

indicators.note: something moving changes position, so the letters shift about

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, ignoring the apostrophe

clue.text: Some basic hormones classically coursing through the veins

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun

explanation.walkthrough: 'Classically' marks the definition as belonging to Greek myth rather than modern physiology.

clue.text: Natural to be present in pub at end of shift

the final letter only

clue.text: Remarkably absorbent fleece finally found in front of cage

indicators.note: remarkably means unusually, so the letters take an unusual order
finally points to the very end, so only the last letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter only

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cage' suggests a pet enclosure; it is the ribcage of the body.

clue.text: Hybrid’s terrible wings came into view

arose means appeared

clue.text: More articles churned out that show a measure of warmth

clue.text: New arrival is something significant for a dwarf?

clue.text: Snake native processed into rissole

clue.text: So houses with lots of land, flipping problem, something for the masses?

clue.text: Dust often associated with these trees

clue.text: One who owns there is no end to decent behaviour by men

clue.text: Back opinion by paper that shows what may come to pass

clue.text: Marine creature, large, eating female that’s cast up on the beach

L for large

clue.text: A series of blows that may bring someone round

a cricket fielder near the boundary rope is placed deep

explanation.surface: A cricketer at the Oval streaking round the field, hanging back near the boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a London cricket ground, and deep fielders stand near the boundary; but this oval is a speed-skating track.
explanation.definitionFit: Long-track racing on ice is held on an oval rink, so a racer there is a competitor on skates.

clue.text: Part of wafer I left with one shell in drink

definitions.note: silicon wafers are sliced into these

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
L for left

a conch is a large spiral seashell
a sip is a small drink

explanation.surface: Someone breaks off a bit of wafer biscuit and leaves a shell in their drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wafer' suggests a biscuit; it is the thin disc of semiconductor from which microchips are cut.
explanation.definitionFit: In chip manufacture a thin disc of crystal is etched with many circuits and diced into individual pieces.
